1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
4	For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
5	Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
6	At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
7	When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
8	
9	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
10	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
11	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
12	\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
13	LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
14	In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
15	This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
16	A controlled ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.
17	Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.
18	
19	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
20	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
21	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
22	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
23	
24	\paragraph{Score compression is task-inherent.}\label{sec:ablation}
25	A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
26	We test this via controlled ablation: generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
27	LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%).
28	NER selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained).
29	This rules out constrained decoding as the cause of compression and establishes LP compression as inherent to structured output generation.
30	The correlation-selection gap is therefore a fundamental challenge for test-time scaling in structured IE, not an artifact of any particular decoding strategy.
31	Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.
32	
33	\paragraph{What drives the universal gap?}
34	Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms.
35	First, the free-form ablation exposes a task-specific interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that is universal across all 7 relation types and driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
36	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
37	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
38	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); multi-seed replication is left for future work.
39	Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
40	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
41	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.
42	
43	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
44	The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
45	Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
46	Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.386$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
47	Our findings are established under constrained decoding with a single-dataset ablation suggesting the gap is intrinsic; whether this generalizes across decoding regimes, datasets, and model scales warrants further investigation.
48

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
A controlled ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Score compression is task-inherent.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation: generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%).
NER selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained).
This rules out constrained decoding as the cause of compression and establishes LP compression as inherent to structured output generation.
The correlation-selection gap is therefore a fundamental challenge for test-time scaling in structured IE, not an artifact of any particular decoding strategy.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.

\paragraph{What drives the universal gap?}
Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms.
First, the free-form ablation exposes a task-specific interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that is universal across all 7 relation types and driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); multi-seed replication is left for future work.
Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.386$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
Our findings are established under constrained decoding with a single-dataset ablation suggesting the gap is intrinsic; whether this generalizes across decoding regimes, datasets, and model scales warrants further investigation.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances annotated for joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types).
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences with 4 entity types, where models achieve ${\approx}$91\% micro F1.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 social media instances with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries (52\% zero F1).
12	
13	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
14	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures, ensuring comparisons across the two model families (both at 8B scale) reflect model differences rather than training confounds.
15	We note a training confound for SciERC: Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), which prepends empty \texttt{<think>\textbackslash n</think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) to each training response and includes them in the loss computation; CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 checkpoints explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}.
16	No reasoning content is present (the blocks are always empty), and constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, so thinking tokens do not appear in generated samples.
17	This constitutes a minor train--test distribution mismatch for SciERC ($<$0.3\% of the 2048-token training window); CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 are unaffected.
18	We discuss implications in the Limitations section.
19	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary; single seed, seed${=}42$), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ results for CoNLL (Qwen) and SciERC (LLaMA) are in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}). A 3-seed stability analysis ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}, Appendix~\ref{app:multiseed}) confirms that signal rankings are identical across seeds.}
20	Quality estimation uses Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; downstream utility uses best-of-$N$ selection F1 with exact span matching (NER) and head-tail-label matching (RE).
21	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
22	
23	%% ============================================================
24	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
25	\label{sec:qe_results}
26	
27	\begin{table*}[t]
28	\centering
29	\small
30	\caption{Quality estimation across tasks and models (Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; $N{=}8$, seed${=}42$). Best value per column in \textbf{bold}. SciERC evaluates joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types, single benchmark---preliminary); CoNLL evaluates NER (4 types). $N{=}16$ results appear in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).}
31	\label{tab:quality_estimation}
32	\begin{tabular}{ll cc cc cc cc}
33	\toprule
34	& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC NER}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC RE}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (Qwen)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (LLaMA)}} \\
35	\cmidrule(lr){3-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-8} \cmidrule(lr){9-10}
36	Signal & Family & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC \\
37	\midrule
38	VC & Structural & \textbf{.379} & .684 & \textbf{.350} & .693 & .424 & .789 & .426 & .709 \\
39	SJ  & Structural & .360 & .692 & .250 & .670 & .436 & .801 & \textbf{.431} & .704 \\
40	FK & Surface & .267 & .629 & .275 & .609 & .400 & .774 & .428 & .703 \\
41	EM  & Surface    & .295 & \textbf{.749} & .134 & \textbf{.706} & \textbf{.451} & \textbf{.816} & \textbf{.431} & .705 \\
42	LP     & Model      & .205 & .578 & .266 & .600 & .316 & .753 & .307 & \textbf{.761} \\
43	\bottomrule
44	\end{tabular}
45	\end{table*}
46	
47	\begin{figure*}[t]
48	\centering
49	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_signal_heatmap}
50	\caption{Quality estimation heatmap (Spearman $\rho$) across five signals and four configurations. Left: full evaluation set; right: conditional set (non-zero F1 instances). On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while LP RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.011$).}
51	\label{fig:signal_heatmap}
52	\end{figure*}
53	
54	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents rank correlation ($\rho$) and AUROC for five confidence signals across tasks and models.
55	
56	\paragraph{Difficulty-dependent signal complementarity.}
57	On SciERC NER (complex schema, 6 types), structural signals lead: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.379$ and SJ $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and LP ($\rho{=}0.205$).
58	This advantage persists on RE (VC $\rho{=}0.350$; preliminary, single benchmark), though all signals weaken due to the 40\% zero-F1 floor effect.
59	VC and SJ show moderate instance-level correlation (NER: $\rho{=}0.659$; RE: $\rho{=}0.605$), indicating information overlap but not redundancy; their differential behavior across difficulty levels reflects the complementary granularity of entity-level frequency vs.\ span-level set overlap.
60	While the best $\rho{=}0.38$ (VC) explains approximately 14\% of F1 variance, the best AUROC reaches 0.749 (EM), indicating strong binary discriminative power for the quality/failure classification most relevant to practitioners in quality-aware routing.\footnote{Semantic entropy \cite{kuhn2023semantic} achieves comparable AUROC on discrete-answer QA; direct comparison is not meaningful due to different output spaces.}
61	Pairwise bootstrap CIs confirm the SJ advantage over LP ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$, CI excludes zero) but not over EM ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$, marginal under Bonferroni correction; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci}, Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
62	
63	\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
64	Signal choice depends on the intended use: on NER, EM leads AUROC (0.749) despite ranking third in $\rho$ (0.295), preferred for binary quality triage; structural signals ($\rho{\geq}0.36$) are better for fine-grained ranking.
65	On CoNLL with LLaMA, LP leads AUROC (0.761) yet trails in $\rho$ (0.307), confirming this pattern across datasets.
66	
67	\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
68	On CoNLL (greedy F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$), surpassing SJ and VC.
69	When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
70	This crossover---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates difficulty-dependent complementarity rather than a universal structural advantage, suggesting practitioners should match signal type to expected task difficulty.
71	Stability across the two model families (both 8B) is strong: SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $0.431$ (LLaMA) on CoNLL ($\Delta{=}0.005$, within 3-seed $\sigma{\approx}0.007$).
72	On WNUT-17, where 52\% of instances receive zero F1, full-set correlations are misleading: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$), but this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
73	LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$, AUROC${=}0.219$).
74	We hypothesize that this reversal reflects overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs \citep{xiong2024llm}: the model assigns high log-probabilities to fluent but incorrect entity patterns (e.g., common noun phrases that resemble but do not match rare WNUT entity types), while producing lower scores for genuinely uncertain outputs where it correctly hedges.
75	On the conditional set, all signals collapse toward weak or non-significant correlations ($\rho{\leq}0.35$), with SJ achieving only $\rho{=}0.089$ ($p{=}0.020$) on the full set---suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency signals capture binary success/failure but not quality gradation.
76	
77	\paragraph{Conditional filtering.}
78	Filtering to non-zero F1 instances reshuffles rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
79	EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$; preliminary), while VC and FK drop substantially (VC NER: $0.379{\to}0.300$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
80	LP RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.011$, confirming its full-set correlation was driven by zero/non-zero separation.
81	This creates a natural complementarity: VC and SJ are preferred on the full set, while EM provides the most precise ranking within the non-trivial subset (see Appendix~\ref{app:additional} for details).
82	
83	%% ============================================================
84	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
85	\label{sec:selection_gap}
86	
87	\begin{figure*}[t]
88	\centering
89	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_selection_gap}
90	\caption{The correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Left: NER; right: RE. Bars show best-of-$N$ selection F1; the line marks quality estimation $\rho$. Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal significantly outperforms greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER LP, the best signal; Table~\ref{tab:selection}). Dashed line indicates oracle upper bound.}
91	\label{fig:selection_gap}
92	\end{figure*}
93	
94	\begin{table}[t]
95	\centering
96	\small
97	\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection F1 on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). RE results are from a single benchmark (preliminary). Best non-oracle result per column in \textbf{bold}. EM selects the plurality output; despite a 42\% pairwise exact-match rate, EM selection underperforms greedy on both tasks.}
98	\label{tab:selection}
99	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
100	\toprule
101	Method & NER F1 & RE F1 \\
102	\midrule
103	Oracle & 0.776 & 0.585 \\
104	\midrule
105	LP           & \textbf{0.650} & 0.395 \\
106	SJ       & 0.645 & 0.386 \\
107	EM        & 0.636 & 0.372 \\
108	VC                 & 0.634 & 0.359 \\
109	\midrule
110	Greedy ($T{=}0$)   & 0.644 & \textbf{0.404} \\
111	Random             & 0.608 & 0.354 \\
112	\bottomrule
113	\end{tabular}
114	\end{table}
115	
116	Despite strong quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited gains when used for best-of-$N$ selection (Table~\ref{tab:selection}, Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
117	Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input regardless of which sample is evaluated; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
118	The non-trivial question is whether log-probability---the only per-sample signal---can exploit the oracle headroom.
119	We anchor this analysis on SciERC, where output diversity is substantial: only 11--18\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N{=}8$ samples, with 39--43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct outputs), per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.11--0.14, and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
120

100	\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}
101	
102	\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
103	RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
104	\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
105	The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
106	We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.
107	
108	\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
109	For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
110	The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
111	For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
112	Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
113	For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
114	On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
115	Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.
116	
117	\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
118	Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

127	\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
128	Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
129	Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
130	Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
131	Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
132	Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
133	Evaluation circularity is negligible.
134	
135	\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
136	On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
137	At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
138	EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
139	On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
140	On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
141	The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

189	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
190	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
191	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
192	Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
193	This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
194	For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
195	The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

368	\paragraph{Prompt template.}
369	For NER, we use a structured prompt:
370	\begin{quote}
371	\small
372	\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
373	\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
374	Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
375	Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
376	\end{quote}
377	RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.
378	
379	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
380	Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
381	This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

383	\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}
384	
385	Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}).
386	The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
387	At $\varepsilon{=}0.05$, 60.3\% of instances have a within-sample range below the threshold, leaving LP unable to meaningfully distinguish candidates.
388	For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold---SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.

408	Among instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total), log-probability selection \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp F1, $p{=}0.01$), and within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied subset).
409	This confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information but is resolution-limited---the signal exists but is compressed below the discrimination threshold for most instances.
410	A free-form decoding ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}) confirms this compression is intrinsic, not decoding-regime-specific.

525	\section{LP Selection Failure Stability}\label{app:lp_failure_stability}
526	
527	We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

529	\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}

531	The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), confirming a stable failure core.
532	
533	\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
534	Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
535	Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher greedy F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429), indicating that LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well---precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.

652	\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
653	When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.386$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.083$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.364$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.014$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.254$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.031$).
654	The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (greedy F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.
655	
656	\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
657	The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
658	The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (greedy NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
659	Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
660	These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs---a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}), not evidence against signal utility.
661	
662	\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
663	The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
664	This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_temperature_robustness}
\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. LP $T{=}0.7$ data unavailable.}
\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.388 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.028 whose bootstrap confidence interval includes zero.
FK shows mixed behavior: NER $\rho$ drops by 0.054, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
Across all comparisons, the SJ--FK relative ordering is preserved at both temperatures on NER (0.388 vs.\ 0.321 at $T{=}0.7$; 0.360 vs.\ 0.267 at $T{=}1.0$), indicating a stable signal hierarchy despite numerically small temperature effects.

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.411{\pm}0.010$ (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of $+0.047$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent---LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$---though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.030$ (range: $+0.027$ to $+0.032$) while LP gains only $+0.003$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.030$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.034$).
SJ, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows setting-dependent variation, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.
At $N{=}16$, SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) while exhibiting lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$), making it a more stable alternative at higher sample sizes.

\paragraph{Transfer across model families.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct replicates the structural-over-surface ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.325{\pm}0.021$, FK $\rho{=}0.256{\pm}0.024$).
On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to greedy within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are anchored to oracle headroom (13--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$---the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST---ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to greedy (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ greedy F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46), indicating that failures are partially systematic---driven by instance complexity---but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), confirming a stable failure core.

\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher greedy F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429), indicating that LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well---precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.

\section{Cross-Dataset OOD Analysis}\label{app:ood}

To test whether confidence signals generalize under domain shift, we evaluate models on out-of-distribution data: a SciERC-trained model applied to CoNLL instances (wider$\to$narrower schema) and vice versa (Table~\ref{tab:ood}).

\centering

FK & .285\textsuperscript{***} & .254 & +.031 & $-$.070 & .254 & $-$.324 \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.386$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.083$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.364$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.014$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.254$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.031$).
The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (greedy F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (greedy NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs---a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}), not evidence against signal utility.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

content.text:
Now I have all the information needed. Let me compile the findings.

Here is my item-by-item assessment:

---

**1. R3-W6 (first multi-family claim): PASS**

No "first" claim found anywhere in `introduction.tex` or either `abstract.tex`. The introduction says "We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families" and "Our work extends theirs [Nedellec et al.] in three directions." The framing is comparative/systematic, not priority-claiming. The abstracts likewise contain no "first" language. The claim has been appropriately softened.

**2. R3-W7 (VC/Voting Conf terminology): PASS**

The abbreviation "VC" is introduced formally in `introduction.tex` line 35 as "entity voting confidence [VC]" and consistently used as "VC" throughout all files thereafter. The notation table in `appendix.tex` defines "VC ($c_{\mathrm{vc}}$) = Entity voting confidence." The method section (`method.tex` line 57) introduces it as "Entity voting confidence (structural, instance-level)." The full phrase "voting confidence" does not appear without the "entity" prefix or the abbreviation, and "VC" is used consistently as the shorthand. Terminology is consistent.

**3. R5-W1 (Qwen3 thinking token): PASS**

The paper explicitly discusses `enable_thinking` in three locations:
- `experiments.tex` lines 15-18: Full disclosure that SciERC checkpoint used `enable_thinking=True`, blocks are empty, constrained decoding suppresses them at inference.
- `limitations.tex` lines 18-21: Detailed discussion of the confound, acknowledging empty blocks may weakly affect LP calibration but the gap is not explained by it since CoNLL/WNUT lack the confound.
- `appendix.tex` line 381 (training config footnote): Cross-reference to the confound.

The issue is thoroughly addressed.

**4. R5-W2 (semantic entropy footnote): PASS**

In `experiments.tex` line 60, there is a footnote: "Semantic entropy \cite{kuhn2023semantic} achieves comparable AUROC on discrete-answer QA; direct comparison is not meaningful due to different output spaces." Additionally, `related_work.tex` line 21 discusses semantic uncertainty with citation to `kuhn2023semantic` and its probe distillation (`kossen2024semantic`). The `references.bib` contains the correct Kuhn et al. 2023 entry (ICLR 2023). Properly addressed.

**5. R5-W3 (bib mismatch he2024uncertainty): PASS**

The `references.bib` entry for `he2024uncertainty` (lines 88-95) reads:
- Title: "Uncertainty Estimation on Sequential Labeling via Uncertainty Transmission"
- Authors: He, Jianfeng; Yu, Linlin; Lei, Shuo; Lu, Chang-Tien; Chen, Feng
- Venue: Findings of NAACL 2024, pages 2823-2835
- DOI: 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.180

This is a real paper with a valid ACL Anthology DOI. The entry looks correct and complete.

**6. R5-M4 (bib OpenAlex issues): PASS (with minor note)**

No OpenAlex URLs or identifiers found in the bib file. All URLs point to arXiv, ACL Anthology, or publisher DOIs. The entries have proper venue information. One minor note: `chen2024usc` has `booktitle = {arXiv preprint (ICML 2024 Workshop ICL)}` which mixes arXiv preprint format with a workshop mention -- slightly unconventional but not an OpenAlex artifact. Overall, the bibliography appears hand-curated or properly cleaned, with no auto-generated OpenAlex-style entries.

**7. R5-M5 (Ethics Statement): PASS**

`main.tex` lines 39-43 contain a substantive ethics statement covering:
- All benchmarks are publicly available (SciERC, CoNLL-2003, WNUT-17)
- Open-weight models used
- CoNLL-2003's Reuters/NIST provenance noted
- No new human data collected
- Positive framing of findings for reliable IE deployment

This is substantive, not boilerplate.

**8. R4-M3 (Table 1 N=16 blank): PASS**

Table 1 (`tab:quality_estimation` in `experiments.tex` lines 27-45) only shows N=8 results. N=16 data is not inline in this table -- it is explicitly delegated via footnote (line 19) and table caption (line 30) to Table `tab:robustness` in Appendix `app:robustness`. The main Table 1 has no blank cells; all 5 signals x 8 columns are filled. The appendix robustness table (`appendix.tex` lines 31-60) also has no blanks -- LLaMA CoNLL RE shows "---" which is intentional (RE not evaluated on CoNLL). No N=16 blank-cell issue exists.

**9. R6-W2 (Figure 1 caption): PASS**

Figure 1 (`fig:overview` in `introduction.tex` lines 28-33) has a concise two-sentence caption: "The correlation-selection gap. **Left**: high inter-sample agreement correlates with high F1 (quality estimation). **Right**: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates, precluding sample selection." This is brief and informative, not overly verbose or redundant.

---

**IMPORTANT CAVEAT**: There are two `discussion.tex` files. The one in `sections/discussion.tex` (used by `main.tex` via `\input{sections/discussion}`) is the current version with the free-form ablation results integrated. However, the root-level `discussion.tex` is an older version that still contains `\textit{[Planned experiment: free-form ablation on SciERC NER/RE.]}` on line 26 and lacks the ablation results. Since `main.tex` inputs from `sections/`, the compiled paper uses the correct version, but the stale root-level file is a cleanup issue worth noting.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
A controlled ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed), suggesting that constrained decoding may be a contributing factor for RE even though it is not for NER.
The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific rather than universal.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); multi-seed replication is left for future work.
Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.386$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
Our findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
Whether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We systematically evaluate five confidence signals across quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection for LLM-based structured IE, revealing that these metrics decouple---single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) yet none significantly improves sample selection despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
The instance-level failure of four signals is definitional; the empirical finding is that neither consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) nor log-probability bridges the gap.
MBR utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them; LP scores are compressed into effective ties (60\% of instances), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
A controlled free-form decoding ablation confirms that NER LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, LP selection reverses direction (preliminary), indicating task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
Signal rankings shift with task difficulty---EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude; at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse to non-significance.
RE findings rest on SciERC alone (preliminary) and warrant multi-benchmark validation.
Trained verifiers, scaling to 70B+ models, and conformal prediction are promising directions for closing the gap.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work extends theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs from general-purpose models are unparseable.\footnote{Fine-tuned models may retain format compliance without grammar constraints: our free-form ablation achieves 99.95\% valid JSON rate (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).}
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction---this is definitional, not empirical.
The non-trivial questions are whether (a)~consensus-proximity selection, instantiating MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high, muller2021understanding}, can recover per-sample discrimination, and (b)~whether log-probability, the only per-sample signal, can exploit the headroom.
Both fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); log-probability scores are severely compressed (60\% of instances effectively tied), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
A controlled free-form decoding ablation confirms that NER LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, LP selection reverses direction (preliminary), revealing task-dependent interaction with decoding regime (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: high inter-sample agreement correlates with high F1 (quality estimation). \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates, precluding sample selection.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Evaluation framework and metric dissociation.}
    We compare five confidence signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection.
    These metrics decouple: EM leads AUROC (0.749) but ranks third in $\rho$ (0.295), demonstrating that single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.

    \item \textbf{Diagnosing why selection fails beyond definitional limitations.}
    Four of five signals are instance-level by definition and cannot rank candidates---this is not an empirical finding.
    The empirical contribution is diagnosing why the two mechanisms that \textit{could} bridge the gap both fail: (a)~consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) correlates with quality across instances but not within them; (b)~log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties (60\% of instances within $\varepsilon{=}0.05$), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
    A controlled NER ablation confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, LP selection reverses direction (preliminary), suggesting task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
    At the capability boundary (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance and LP exhibits strong negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---phenomena invisible on a single dataset that extend \citet{nedellec2026consistency}'s quality-estimation analysis.
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction (IE), but whether confidence signals can identify the best output among multiple candidates remains untested for structured tasks.
We evaluate five confidence signals on three NER benchmarks and one RE benchmark with two 8B-parameter model families.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) yet none significantly improves sample selection despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom---a \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
For four of five signals, selection failure follows from their definition as instance-level scores; the empirical question is whether per-sample log-probability or consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) can bridge the gap.
Neither succeeds: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties within instances, and MBR utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
A controlled ablation on NER confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, LP selection reverses direction, suggesting task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
These findings, consistent across two model families at 8B scale, indicate that closing the gap likely requires per-sample scoring beyond unsupervised signals.
\end{abstract}
